title: Why food is the whole story of Indian inflation
tension: In India, inflation more or less IS food inflation. Nearly half the basket is food, so a failed monsoon or an onion shock can set the entire country's cost of living and shake governments. And the cruelty is built in: the poorer you are, the more of your money goes on eating, so the people with the least feel the price of a tomato first and hardest. The RBI can raise interest rates all it likes, but no repo rate ever grew an onion.
teachingGoal: Show why food dominates Indian inflation and what that means: food's near-half weight (and why, via Engel's law), how volatile food is and which items swing it, why that volatility is driven by weather and supply not money, why interest rates are nearly powerless against it, who it hurts most, and why food prices are political dynamite. The reader should understand the gap between the food a household feels and the headline number.
sectionArc: Why does food matter so much more in India? (food and beverages about 37% of the current 2024 basket, down from 46% and still the largest by far, versus a small slice in rich countries; Engel's law, and the very fact that food's weight just fell is Engel's law unfolding in real time)
How much does food move the headline? (food's contribution to inflation; how the headline lurches when food does; the consumer food price measure)
Why is food so volatile? (monsoon, perishables, supply shocks; the items that spike, vegetables, pulses, edible oils, onions and tomatoes; this is weather and supply, not money printing)
Why can't the RBI just fix it with interest rates? (rate hikes cool demand, but food inflation is mostly supply-side; raising rates does not grow onions; the dilemma this creates for monetary policy)
Who gets hurt the most? (poorer and rural households spend more of their income on food, so food inflation is a regressive shock; rural versus urban food inflation)
Why food prices are political dynamite (buffer stocks, minimum support prices, export and stock limits; the 'onion price' that has helped topple state governments)
So what does food inflation really tell you? (it is the lived cost of living for most Indians, often diverging from the calm-looking headline; watch food)
mustTeach: food and beverages is nearly half of India's CPI basket, far higher than in rich countries, because poorer households spend a larger share on food (Engel's law)
food is highly volatile and can dominate swings in the headline number
food inflation is mostly supply-driven (monsoon, perishables, shocks), not monetary
interest rates are weak against supply-driven food inflation, which complicates monetary policy
poorer and rural households are hit hardest because food is a bigger share of their spending
food prices are politically explosive and managed with buffer stocks, MSPs and trade controls

CURRENCY (important): the current official basket is the 2024-base series, launched 12 Feb 2026. Use the 2024 weights (food and beverages 36.75%) as the CURRENT weights, and cite the old 2012 weights only to show what changed. The detailed month-by-month component inflation figures (vegetables, onion, etc.) come from the longer 2012-base series and must be framed as recent readings under the previous basket, never invented for the new base.

contextCards.fact: Engel's law: as households grow richer they spend a smaller SHARE of their income on food, even as they spend more in absolute terms. So food's large weight in India's CPI basket is itself a sign that most Indians are not rich, and it means food inflation lands hardest on the poorest, for whom food is the biggest line in the budget.
contextCards.source: Engel's law (Ernst Engel; standard, widely established)

contextCards.fact: Governments treat food inflation as a political emergency, not just an economic one. They manage it with buffer stocks of grain, minimum support prices for farmers, and occasional bans or limits on exports and stockholding. The price of staples like onions and tomatoes has repeatedly become an election issue and has been blamed for the fall of state governments, which is why food-price spikes draw fast, sometimes clumsy, policy intervention.
contextCards.source: Indian food-price policy (buffer stocks, MSP, export bans); 'onion politics' (widely documented)

contextCards.fact: On 12 February 2026 India launched a new Consumer Price Index series with base year 2024 (replacing 2012), built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24. The biggest change: the weight of food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 36.75%, because Indians now spend a smaller share of their budgets on food and more on services, a textbook case of Engel's law. Housing and utilities rose to about 17.7%, transport and communication to about 12.4%, and health to about 6.1%. The basket grew from 299 to 358 items, adding e-commerce and online prices, telecom data plans and OTT streaming subscriptions for the first time, and switched to the international COICOP classification of 12 divisions instead of the old six groups. Headline inflation on the new base was 2.75% in January 2026.
contextCards.source: MoSPI / NSO, first CPI release on base 2024=100, 12 February 2026; HCES 2023-24
